# CloudBitmaps

> Distributed, cloud-native Roaring Bitmaps. Query and intersect billion-scale integer sets over tiered
> cloud storage (RAM → warm NoSQL/SQL → cold immutable objects) at a fraction of an always-on cache, with
> the familiar in-memory API: `add`, `has`, `remove`, `count`, `intersect`.

CloudBitmaps maps each 16-bit Roaring chunk onto pluggable cloud storage tiers. The distinguishing capability
is **serverless chunk-skipping intersection**: `A ∩ B` fetches only the chunks that can possibly contribute,
so intersecting two 2,000,000-id segments touches only the shared chunks, and `count()` on a published
segment does zero payload reads.

Install `@cloudbitmaps/roaring` — `@cloudbitmaps/core` (the codec-agnostic engine plus all ten storage
drivers) arrives transitively. Ten backends ship as optional-peer subpaths: S3, GCS, Azure Blob, DynamoDB,
Postgres, Redis, MongoDB, Cassandra, MySQL, and local filesystem.

## Measured, not modelled

Benchmarked against real S3 + DynamoDB in us-east-1 — not an emulator — with DynamoDB capacity taken from
AWS's own ConsumedCapacity: $0.75 per million incremental writes, $0.14 per million count()s, $5.88 per
million segment publishes, against an always-on Redis-HA line of $346/month standing.

## Coming from Redis bitmaps

A durable alternative to Redis bitmaps for set-shaped workloads — audiences, dedup, suppression, membership —
where the sets are large, mostly idle, must survive a restart, and are written in batches. Operations map
one-for-one for everything set-shaped: SETBIT/GETBIT/BITCOUNT become add|addMany/has/count, BITOP AND/OR/DIFF
become intersect/union/andNot, and `prior = SETBIT` becomes claimMany(ids), which adds a batch and returns only
the ids that were not already present (the exactly-once dedup primitive; one write per 65,536-id chunk rather
than one per id).

Not a drop-in replacement, and the two limits are load-bearing rather than footnotes:

1. No addressable-bit surface. BITPOS, BITFIELD, byte-range BITCOUNT and BITOP NOT have no equivalent — this is
   a set of ids, not a positional bit buffer, and NOT has no bounded universe to complement against. The raw
   bytes are not interoperable either: a .crbm object is not a flat bit array, and raw bit-position import is
   not built.
2. Do not port a per-id write loop. SETBIT flips one bit in place and is O(1); here a warm write re-serializes
   a whole 65,536-id chunk. Measured: 5,000 ids added one at a time cost 5,000 writes and 23,762 KB, against 1
   write and 8 KB for the same ids in one call — roughly 3,000x the bytes. Batched, it is far cheaper than
   Redis; looped, far more expensive. What that costs depends on the backend's pricing model: a direct line item
   on per-request metered stores (DynamoDB on-demand), consumed throughput and throttling on provisioned
   capacity, and IOPS/CPU/latency headroom rather than an invoice line on instance-priced stores (ElastiCache,
   RDS, Atlas).

Retention is per segment and built in: setRetention(ref, {expiresAt}) records when a segment becomes eligible
for retirement, and retireExpired() is the sweep that acts on it, retiring each expired segment through
dropSegment. The expiry is an absolute instant the writer sets, not a duration derived from anything observed,
because compaction rewrites every basis such a duration could use. The sweep is a function you schedule -- this
library starts no timer, so the same code behaves identically in a Lambda, an edge isolate and a long-running
server. There is no per-id TTL: a bitmap stores ids, not timestamps, and a per-id timestamp costs more than the
compression saves. Never enable a backend's native row expiry on the warm table -- a data-loss footgun, because
warm rows are un-compacted deltas. No seed step is
required — a segment with no cold generation and no registry row is fully functional — and compaction is a cost
optimization, never a correctness requirement.

Redis also remains supported as a warm tier underneath, so "replacing Redis bitmaps" means replacing
SETBIT-on-one-giant-key as the data model, not necessarily replacing Redis as infrastructure.

## When NOT to use it

If you need a sub-millisecond p99 on a working set that fits a bounded hot cache, use Redis: a check that
misses the hot cache costs a network round trip, where an in-process RAM store costs a memory read. CloudBitmaps is for sets
that are large, mostly read, and shouldn't cost $346/month to keep warm. In-region latency is not yet
calibrated and no in-region figure is published.

## Status

v0.9.0, Apache-2.0, published tokenlessly with SLSA build provenance. Pre-1.0: breaking changes are possible
in a minor bump until the .crbm format freezes at 1.0.
